---
title: Build on other apps
description: Ship an app that uses other apps, either created with it or already running, upgrade them together, and act in another app as the person who uses yours.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**Task:** build an app on top of others: an app that brings its own database app,
or a plugin, such as a booking page, that works on a calendar its user already runs.

Three things make this work, and an app can use any of them:

- **References.** Your release names the apps it uses, in its signed manifest.
- **Links.** The node tells your code which app instance answers to each reference.
- **Grants.** The person lets your app call another app as them, so that app's own
  rules for that person apply.

The other app needs no support for any of it. It sees an ordinary call from you,
or a call from its own user.

## 1. Name the apps you use

Each reference has a name your code uses, the package it means and the versions it
takes. Put them in your crate's `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package.metadata.calimero.uses]
kv = { package = "com.calimero.confidential-kv", range = "^0.1", mode = "create" }
calendar = { package = "com.example.calendar", range = "^2", mode = "attach", methods = ["listEvents", "createEvent"] }
```

- `mode = "create"`: each instance of your app gets its own, made with it.
- `mode = "attach"`: the owner points the reference at an app they already run.
- `methods`: what your app calls there **as the person** it serves, once they allow
  it ([step 5](#5-act-as-the-person)). Leave it out to call only as your app.

`meroctl app pack` signs them into the release and checks every method against the
target's vendored ABI. The node checks the rest at install (`400 BAD_USES`), shows
the references on the release's capability card, and an upgrade's consent page
names the apps a new release starts using or uses differently. The full rules are in
[Packaging and signing](/build/packaging-signing/).

Three example apps in core's `apps/` show each step, with harness tests:

- [`calendar`](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/tree/master/apps/calendar): the app
  the other two use. It keeps each caller's events, and `env::via()` keeps a person's
  private events from an app acting for them.
- [`planner`](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/tree/master/apps/planner): `create`.
  Each planner comes with its own calendar and calls it as itself.
- [`booking`](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/tree/master/apps/booking): `attach`
  plus delegation. The owner attaches a calendar, and with a person's grant a booking lands
  in their own calendar.

## 2. Use an app created with your instance

When someone creates an instance of your release, the node first creates each
`create` reference in the same organization, owned by the same person, and named
`<instance>.<name>`. Your `init` can take their ids:

```rust
#[app::init]
pub fn init(links: Option<BTreeMap<String, String>>) -> app::Result<Self> { .. }
```

Any method can read a link at any time with `env::linked`:

```rust
pub fn put(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
    // `Error::NoKv` is a variant of your `#[app::error]` enum.
    let kv = env::linked("kv").ok_or_else(|| Error::NoKv.into())?;
    let args = std::collections::BTreeMap::from([("key", key), ("value", value)]);
    env::xcall(&kv, "set", &args)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The member must admit your app, like any app called by another
([Cross-app calls](/build/guides/cross-context/#1-admit-the-caller)).

## 3. Use an app the owner already runs

An `attach` reference starts empty. The owner fills it with an app they manage in the
same organization, confirming with their passkey:

```http
PUT /apps/{your-app}/links/calendar  { "app": "<their calendar's id>" }
```

`DELETE` on the same path detaches it, and deleting the calendar detaches it too.
`GET /apps/{your-app}/links` lists every reference, the app linked under it, the
release that app runs and whether that release is inside your range (`inRange`).

Read the link each time you call. The owner may attach another app later, or none:

```rust
let Some(calendar) = env::linked("calendar") else {
    app::bail!(Error::NoCalendar); // attach a calendar first
};
```

## 4. Upgrade together

The apps your instance created upgrade with it, in one approval:

- **From your frontend:** ask the node's consent page with
  `upgradeUnit { app, toVersion }`. It shows every app's changes on one page.
- **From a client:** call `POST /apps/{app}/upgrade-unit { version }`.

Each member moves to the release your new version pins for it, else the newest
installed one inside its range. A member cannot be upgraded on its own outside the
range your instance takes it with (`409 OUTSIDE_UNIT_RANGE`).

An attached app is never upgraded with yours: it is the owner's own. When a new
release of yours takes it in another range, the upgrade's consent page warns them.

## 5. Act as the person

By default your call reaches the other app as your app (`Caller::App`), and it never
learns whom you were serving. To work on the calendar as its user, for example to
book into their own calendar with their own permissions there, the person allows it
once:

1. Your release lists the methods in the reference's `methods` (step 1).
2. Your frontend asks the node's consent page with `delegate { app, target }`.
   The page names both apps and every method, and the person confirms with their
   passkey. Your frontend cannot grant this through the API by itself.
3. From then on, when that person's call runs your app, your calls of those methods
   reach the calendar **as the person**.

The calendar needs no change. It sees its own user calling, with its usual rules.
If it wants to treat a call through another app differently, `env::via()` names the
app it came through:

```rust
pub fn create_event(&mut self, event: Event) -> app::Result<()> {
    let env::Caller::Account(who) = env::caller() else {
        return Err(AppError::forbidden());
    };
    if env::via().is_some() && event.private {
        // Through a plugin, only public events.
        return Err(AppError::forbidden());
    }
    self.events.insert(&event.id, &Event { owner: who, ..event })?;
    Ok(())
}
```

A grant covers only the listed methods, and only while the person still reaches
both apps. Anything else runs as your app: another method, a timer, an action, or a
call your app received from another app. A method that needs the person's passkey
confirmation is refused, so a plugin never confirms for them. The person takes the
grant back with `DELETE /apps/{app}/delegations/{target}`, and
`GET /apps/{app}/delegations` lists what they allowed. The protocol is in
[As the person](/protocol/xcall/#as-the-person).

<Aside type="note">
  Creating members, unit upgrades, attaching and grants need every node on
  1.0.0-rc.31 or later. Before that the node refuses them (`409 FEATURE_NOT_ACTIVE`).
</Aside>

## Test it

In the test harness, `TestApp::link(name, Some(app))` sets what `env::linked`
returns, and `deliver_for(from, account, method, args)` runs a delivered call as the
person, with `env::via()` naming `from` ([Testing](/build/testing/)).
